rationale: Closed-form theory does need shortcuts through the dynamics, and historically many fields started with tractable cases. It is not the fundamental reason traditional science made little progress on complex systems: statistical mechanics, continuum mechanics, and evolutionary theory made large advances without reducing every trajectory to a short formula.

Many systems, including chaotic maps and some cellular automata, have no closed form and must be stepped forward explicitly. The further claim that almost any complex-looking behavior has no easy theory is too strong, because coarse-grained, statistical, and scaling descriptions often predict the observed behavior without simulating every degree of freedom.

Rule 60 is an additive cellular automaton whose cell values are binomial coefficients modulo 2, so Lucas's criterion reads them off the binary digits of the time and position in a number of steps logarithmic in t. Rule 188 is a nested rule with a similar digit shortcut, so the stated logarithmic procedure is the right complexity for these patterns.

Among very small programs, behavior that looks complicated but collapses to a short formula does appear uncommon. That does not establish that the vast majority of complex-looking behavior in nature is computationally irreducible, since many natural patterns still have effective equations, conservation laws, or statistical closures.

Deterministic unpredictability does not require external noise, chaos injected from outside, or quantum randomness, and brains are certainly hard to shortcut. Identifying the appearance of free will with irreducible computation is a philosophical conjecture, not a result supported by decision neuroscience or by the usual analyses of responsibility and reasons.

For families of systems rich enough to encode computation, many questions about the infinite-time fate of every initial condition are undecidable. A single natural system is not itself an undecidable problem, and plenty of complex-looking systems have decidable long-run questions, so undecidability is not almost automatic throughout nature.

Very small cellular automata do produce patterns whose lifetimes differ by many orders of magnitude, including transients of thousands to millions of steps from simple seeds. Those long, apparently unsettled lifetimes illustrate practical unpredictability; calling that effect undecidability proper overstates what a finite simulation of one code shows.

The Post correspondence problem is decidable for two pairs and undecidable for the unrestricted problem and for instances with five pairs. Undecidability already at three pairs is a natural suspicion but is not a theorem, so the claim that three pairs make the question undecidable in general is unresolved.

There are exactly 4096 machines under the usual 2-state 2-color encoding in which each of four state-symbol cases chooses a color, a direction, and a state. A complete survey can only see finitely many growth types, and linear, quadratic, and exponential growth, with exponential cases matched by bounded machines for the same function, is a credible census for that tiny class, though it depends on the halting convention.

The count of 4-state 2-color machines is 16 to the eighth, about 4.3 billion, and time-hierarchy arguments show that some computations really do need exponentially many steps. Failure of other machines in that same finite list to shortcut a run is weaker than a proof that no shorter method exists, so the exponential conclusion is only suggested.

The standard universal models, including Turing machines, cellular automata, and tag or substitution systems, simulate one another with polynomial overhead of the stated kind, such as quadratic or dimension-dependent slowdown. Not almost every varied system does so, and extending the comparison to rates of computation in nature remains a conjecture.

The statement is the claim that P differs from NP. That separation is unproved, but worst-case combinatorial search has resisted polynomial algorithms for decades, relativized and natural-proof barriers explain why current techniques stall, and the great majority of complexity theorists expect the classes to differ.

Finite-time inverse problems for cellular automata sit in NP, because a guessed initial row can be checked by direct simulation, and some simple automaton questions are NP-complete. Rule 30 specifically is not known to be universal, and NP-completeness of its inverse problems, including a central black stripe, is an expectation rather than a proof.

The quantum formalism does allow exponential speedups, notably for period-finding, relative to classical Turing machines. Experiments continue to match linear quantum mechanics at the scales relevant to computation, and there is no good evidence that the speedup is only an artifact that ultimate physics will cancel.

For many irreversible or cryptographically hard systems, forward simulation is cheap while searching for a preimage is exponential. The gap is not almost universal among complex-looking systems: linear, integrable, and reversible systems have inverses of essentially the same cost as the forward map.

In any sufficiently strong, consistent, recursively axiomatized theory there are short statements whose shortest proofs are arbitrarily long, by counting and by Gödel speedup when axioms are added. Adding axioms shortens some proofs but recreates the same phenomenon, so short theorems with only long proofs are a genuine feature of ordinary mathematics.

If an axiom system is complete and consistent and theorems can be enumerated, then for each statement one can wait until the statement or its negation appears, deciding every question. Undecidability of long-run reachability in the corresponding multiway system is therefore incompatible with being both complete and consistent, which is Gödel's theorem in that language.

Rule 110 is universal, and every recursively enumerable set, including the histories of a universal cellular automaton, has a Diophantine representation, so arithmetic can encode that computation. A consistent computably axiomatized arithmetic that represents all computable functions is incomplete, though this route is a modern encoding of Gödel's theorem rather than a consequence unique to the principle of computational equivalence.

Several remarkably small rewrite systems and axiom systems are universal, so the threshold can be low. Many theories past any modest complexity threshold remain decidable and non-universal, including Presburger arithmetic, real-closed fields, and abelian groups, so almost every axiom system is not forced into undecidability.

Propositional logic is decidable, a binary predicate makes pure predicate logic undecidable, and arithmetic, set theory, groups, and rings can encode computation, while abelian groups and the elementary theories of the reals and of geometry are decidable. The claim that every axiom system actually used in current research is known to be universal is false, because those decidable theories are in active use.

Universal Diophantine equations are known with on the order of nine variables and enormously many terms, via the representation of recursively enumerable sets by polynomial equations. Incompleteness supplies equations with no solutions that arithmetic cannot prove unsolvable, and the known encodings are so padded that much simpler examples are expected even though they have not been exhibited.

Arithmetic is incomplete, and some number-theoretic statements are independent of the usual axioms. The open problems that number theorists actually work on, such as the Riemann hypothesis, Goldbach's conjecture, and twin primes, are widely expected to be settled in ordinary arithmetic or set theory rather than to form a fair fraction of independence results.

Undecidability does appear in many subjects once the questions are broad enough, including Diophantine equations, word problems, and tilings. It does not begin in practically every area almost as soon as questions stop being easy: large parts of analysis, geometry, and number theory contain deep problems that remain inside decidable or routinely axiomatized mathematics.

Mathematical practice does favor questions its methods can settle, so the published corpus over-represents reducible patches. That selection effect does not make present-day mathematics a small uncharacteristic sample: core subjects pursue problems known to sit next to independence and undecidability, and tractability is not the only filter.

If negation pairs strings of equal length, generating more than half the strings forces some pair to be both proved, and generating fewer than half leaves some pair untouched. Exactly half is not equivalent to completeness plus consistency, because a system can prove both members of one pair and neither member of another and still hit half, unless explosion is assumed and the statement does not assume it.

Peano arithmetic proves the great bulk of ordinary number-theoretic statements, and its nonstandard models differ by infinite integers that rarely affect elementary claims. Widely used systems are not typically close to complete: set theory has central independent statements, and group or ring axioms deliberately admit vastly many non-isomorphic models.

A random short equational theory in one binary operator usually has many nonisomorphic finite models, so it does not pin down a single operation. Boolean algebra, and logic based on a Sheffer stroke, is a genuine exception that forces the operator on a two-element set, which matches the claimed enumeration.

Boolean algebra in the single operation Nand has a one-equation axiomatization using only six Nands, found by searching short equations and confirmed by automated equational proof, and it is far shorter than the classical axiom lists. An axiom that small appears early in any enumeration of the simplest equational systems, so logic would show up among the first few thousand.

Axiom choice is historically contingent, and alternative foundations have founded substantial subjects. Traditional systems are still distinguished by interpretability, consistency strength, and how directly they describe the structures mathematicians use, so it is not the case that nothing fundamental sets them apart or that simple unused systems would routinely yield equally rich fields.

A complexity ordering of propositional tautologies does tend to isolate short independent identities, and many of those match named laws such as de Morgan and excluded middle. Textbooks also name derived and pedagogically useful theorems, so the match to the traditionally highlighted list is only approximate.

Words like powerful or deep loosely track having many consequences or a long chain of ideas, which are network-like features. There is no established correspondence between those intuitions and measured proof networks, and elementary number theory is not well described as a sparse field of isolated facts.

Memory, adaptation, and abstraction can be given senses weak enough to apply to automata or fluids, but those stretched senses are not the marks used in psychology or artificial intelligence. Workable general definitions, based on learning, goals, and flexible problem solving, already exclude teacups and elementary cellular automata without listing human idiosyncrasies.

Self-reproduction, spontaneous pattern formation, and high complexity all occur in simple cellular automata and chemical systems. Standard accounts of life still use general features that those systems lack, including sustained metabolism, hereditary variation, and open-ended Darwinian evolution, so recognition is not limited to Earth-specific details.

Engineers usually select designs whose behavior they can anticipate, which favors modular, computationally reducible structure, and many natural objects lack that constraint. The tendency is real but not uniform: cities, software, and organisms under domestication are human-made and complex, while crystals, orbits, and many organisms look simple.

Behavior alone underdetermines purpose, because the same pattern can be produced by a mechanism with no designer. Minimality is at best a weak hint: evolution and physics often produce compact rules with no purpose, and designed systems are frequently far from minimal.

Efficient compression and encryption remove redundancy, so a communication signal can be statistically indistinguishable from noise, and a search that only looks for narrow carriers would miss it. Beacons meant to be found are the exception and would retain obvious regularities; this is a standard information-theoretic limitation on searches for extraterrestrial signals.

Prime sequences and other sophisticated-looking patterns are generated by tiny non-intelligent programs, so computation by itself is weak evidence of intelligence. The comparison that stellar turbulence quickly outcomputes all of human intellectual history is not a well-defined quantitative fact; it depends on counting microscopic updates as if they were thoughts.

Recognizing intelligence does depend on overlap with capacities we can interpret, and a very alien intelligence could be missed. Sophisticated physical computation is not thereby common in the sense that matters, and it is not established that generalized intelligence is likely and merely bizarre rather than rare.

The space of possible devices is immense, and traditional engineering has concentrated on systems predictable enough to specify and certify. That simple rules with complex behavior will open a vast range of new technology is still a projection: a few decades of work have produced models and curiosities more than a new technological base.

Rule 110 is universal, and computers have been built in many substrates, so in principle a cellular-automaton computer need not use silicon logic gates. A simple chemical process that reliably assembles a rule-110 computer with one or a few atoms per cell is not supported by what is known about error rates, thermal noise, and molecular assembly.

Tiny programs can surprise, and irreducibility blocks any fully general shortcut, so brute-force search is reliable for very small rule spaces. It is not the only reliable route: constraint solvers, probabilistic search, and learning from partial specifications routinely find programs with a requested behavior, and a library of simple programs is not clearly the better technological path.

Universality is a coarse ceiling: many cellular automata, and plausibly some physical systems, can simulate arbitrary computations given enough resources. Resource-bounded capability, learned models, and adaptive control still separate human brains from turbulence and from a single elementary cellular automaton, so equivalence at the universality ceiling does not erase differences in intelligence.

If a process is computationally irreducible, the only general way to obtain all of its consequences is to let it run, so a simple underlying rule would not make every fact predictable by a shortcut. Independent limits from chaos, quantum measurement, and incompleteness already make it very likely that science will not predict everything, whether or not one particular equivalence principle is the right packaging.

With average effects held fixed, the partial change in mean fitness caused by selection equals the additive genetic variance in fitness, in the continuous Malthusian form, and the discrete form divides by mean fitness. This is a theorem of the Price accounting of selection, not an empirical approximation, and it fails only when the stated partial-change conditions are dropped.

For the reaction-diffusion equation with logistic growth, travelling waves exist exactly for speeds at least twice the square root of the product of selection and diffusion, and compact initial data approach that minimal speed. The same pulled-front speed extends to higher dimensions under the stated constant-coefficient assumptions.

Under random mating, autosomal control, and equal parental roles, a parent that invests more in the rarer sex has more grandchildren, so selection equalizes total investment in sons and daughters. When sons and daughters cost the same, that equilibrium is a one-to-one primary sex ratio, and the argument fails where the excluded factors such as local mate competition dominate.

With many unlinked loci of small additive effect, the covariance between relatives is twice the kinship times additive variance plus the dominance term, which recovers the biometric correlations. In the infinite-locus limit the offspring distribution is Gaussian about the midparent with a fixed segregation variance, so Mendelian inheritance produces the continuous patterns biometry had measured.

If a homogeneous steady state of two smooth reactions is stable when well mixed, unequal diffusivities can make some spatial Fourier mode grow when the standard determinant and trace conditions hold. The resulting linear instability is a theorem and is the mechanism that spontaneously generates a spatial pattern from a uniform state.

Near onset on a large domain, the critical wavenumber is fixed by the Jacobian of the reactions and the two diffusivities, and the wavelength scales with the square root of a uniform rescaling of diffusion. Domain size then changes how many repeats fit, rather than setting the spacing, which is the stated selection rule.

Reaction-diffusion of morphogens accounts for some repeated patterns, including aspects of coat markings and pigment stripes. The main phenomena of morphogenesis also depend on gene-regulatory logic, tissue mechanics, growth, cell movement, and simple gradients that are not diffusion-driven instabilities, so reacting and diffusing chemicals are not sufficient for morphogenesis in general.

In the diffusion approximation to a Wright-Fisher population with genic selection, the fixation probability is the stated ratio of exponentials in four times effective size times the selection coefficient, and it reduces to the initial frequency when selection vanishes. A single neutral mutant in a diploid population therefore fixes with probability one over twice the number of gene copies.

Neutral mutants arise at a rate proportional to population size and each fixes with the reciprocal probability, so the substitution rate equals the mutation rate per generation and the population size cancels. A constant per-generation mutation rate then produces a molecular clock measured in generations; a clock in years needs generation time to be comparably stable.

Conditional on fixation, the diffusion approximation gives a mean time of minus four effective sizes times (1-p) log(1-p) over p. For a new neutral mutant, p is one over twice the census size and the expression tends to four times the effective population size in generations.

In the infinite-alleles model at equilibrium, expected heterozygosity is theta over one plus theta, with theta equal to four times effective size times the neutral mutation rate. That quantity increases as population size or mutation rate increases, which is the stated balance between drift and the input of new alleles.

Across whole genomes, especially in species with large amounts of noncoding DNA, most nucleotide substitutions are consistent with drift of neutral or nearly neutral variants. Positive selection drives a substantial minority of changes at functional sites, and in some taxa that minority is large, so the strong claim that most molecular evolution is not adaptive is only partly right.

When fitness effects are additive and selection is weak, a social gene spreads if relatedness times benefit exceeds cost. In the regression form derived from the Price equation the same inequality is a general partition of fitness, so under the stated definitions the rule is a theorem rather than a loose slogan.

Under single mating, haplodiploid full sisters are related by three quarters, more than a mother to her offspring, while sisters are related to brothers by only one quarter. That asymmetry does not by itself predispose sterile castes: at an even sex ratio the average relatedness to siblings is one half, many haplodiploid insects are solitary, and eusociality also evolved in diploids, with monogamy a better predictor than haplodiploidy.

When n foundresses share a patch, sons compete locally, and only daughters disperse, the unbeatable fraction of males is (n-1) over 2n, which is female-biased and rises toward one half as n grows. The result is a standard evolutionarily stable strategy and matches the sex ratios of fig wasps and parasitoids under those life histories.

Hamilton's sensitivity of the growth rate to survival at age a is proportional to the remaining reproductive value and does not increase with age after reproduction starts. That decline makes late deleterious effects hard to remove and is the main evolutionary reason senescence is expected, though it is not mathematically inevitable in every age-structured life history.

The stated payoff conditions are exactly the definition of an evolutionarily stable strategy against any rare alternative in a large well-mixed population. Every such strategy is an asymptotically stable rest point of the replicator dynamics, and there are stable rest points that are not evolutionarily stable, so the converse fails as claimed.

With the standard hawk and dove payoffs, when injury cost exceeds resource value neither pure strategy is stable, and the unique evolutionarily stable mixture plays hawk with probability equal to value over cost. Ownership or other role asymmetries replace that mixture by a bourgeois convention, which the assumptions exclude.

If the longer display wins, cost accrues at a constant rate, and rivals do not signal their choice, the unique evolutionarily stable persistence time is exponential with mean equal to the resource value. That density is the stated one over V times e to the minus x over V, and the assumptions rule out the asymmetries that would change it.

If males contribute no resources, fecundity is equal, and the sex ratio is one to one, an asexual female puts twice as many daughters into the next generation as a sexual female, so the odds of asexuals double each generation. Sex must then have a compensating advantage of up to twofold to resist replacement, which is the standard cost of males.

A selective sweep drags linked neutral alleles to fixation and thereby reduces heterozygosity, and the surviving fraction increases with the ratio of recombination to the selection coefficient, vanishing when linkage is very tight. The region of strong reduction has a width of order the selection coefficient in recombination units, up to logarithmic factors in population size.
